title: An Overview of Apparel Compliance Deductions
summary: A field guide to the apparel compliance deductions retailers use most, including shortage and floor-ready chargebacks, prevention and dispute strategies, and the documents that support it.
body_markdown:
In this article, learn about:


- Why shortage claims dominate the deduction landscape and how many may be incorrect.


- What retailers expect for hangers, tickets, and carton labeling, and what happens when a shipment misses those requirements.


- How to classify a deduction as preventable, disputable, or both.


- How to build a documentation process that supports successful disputes.


A deduction may hit accounting as a smaller payment, but the real cost can be harder to see. Someone has to determine why the money was withheld, whether the retailer is justified, and what (if anything) the brand can do about it.


For emerging and midsize apparel, footwear, and accessories brands, that decision often falls across operations, accounts receivable, and account management. The practical skill is classifying each deduction as preventable, disputable, or both. That classification helps teams focus their effort where it can make a difference, rather than automatically writing off the amount or treating every deduction as disputable.


This guide covers two of the most common areas apparel suppliers encounter: **shortage claims** , which make up a large share of the deduction landscape, and **physical compliance failures** involving hangers, tickets, and carton labeling. For each category, we’ll look at what triggers the deduction, what it costs, whether it’s preventable or disputable, and which documents can support a dispute.


## Preventable, Disputable, or Both?


Some disputes are preventable, some can be disputed to recoup lost funds, and some fall in both categories. This chart breaks it down.


Category


Typical Trigger


Classification


Prevention Strategy


Supporting Dispute Documents


Shortage claims


Retailer’s receiving count is lower than the invoiced quantity.


Mostly disputable; some are preventable.


Keep one purchase order per carton or pallet and match invoiced quantities to shipped quantities.


Advance ship notice, signed bill of lading with driver-noted case count, proof of delivery.


Hanger and ticketing violations


Wrong, unapproved, or missing hanger; unattached or misplaced ticket.


Almost entirely preventable.


Double-check the retailer’s approved hanger and ticket requirements before the first shipment.


Packing slip and hanger specification sheet showing compliance when the deduction misidentifies the shipment.


Carton and labeling errors


Carton size or weight outside spec, missing or unscannable barcode, or mixed purchase orders in one carton.


Mostly preventable.


Test scans before shipment and keep purchase orders separated unless a written exception exists.


Carton contents record and routing guide in effect at ship date.


RFID and private-label ticketing


Missing RFID hangtag or sticker on private-label goods.


Preventable.


Double-check the current RFID vendor and tag-placement requirements before production.


Vendor confirmation of tag application and the retailer’s dated RFID requirement.


## Why Shortage Claims Matter


A shortage claim occurs when a retailer’s receiving count is lower than the quantity the supplier invoiced. According to[The Supply Chain Source](https://supplierwiki.supplypike.com/articles/trade-deductions-and-chargebacks) , shortages make up roughly 80% of off-invoice deductions industry-wide, and many are invalid.


The difference between what shipped and what a retailer records as received can have several causes. Purchase orders may be commingled, a shipment may be received incorrectly, or the paperwork may not match the physical shipment. A shortage deduction, therefore, doesn’t necessarily mean the supplier shipped fewer units than ordered.


### Preventing Shortage Claims


Retailers generally expect suppliers to keep one purchase order per carton or pallet unless a written agreement says otherwise. Combining multiple purchase orders into one shipment without clearly separating them can make it difficult for a retailer to reconcile what arrived. That can lead to a shortage claim even when every unit was shipped.


Suppliers can reduce the risk of these deductions by focusing on three practices:


- Match invoice quantities to the quantities that actually ship.


- Keep purchase orders separated by carton or pallet.


- Have the driver note the case count on the bill of lading (BOL) before the shipment leaves the dock.


Kohl’s provides one example of how this can affect payment. According to[The Supply Chain Source](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/kohls-invoicing-and-ap-deductions-guide) , Kohl’s requires the purchase order, invoice, and receipt to match before it automatically pays an invoice. A split shipment can trigger a shortage deduction for units that haven’t been received yet, even when those units are already in transit.


### Disputing Shortage Claims


The strongest documents for a shortage dispute are the records that show what actually left the supplier’s facility. These typically include the advance ship notice (ASN), a signed BOL with the driver’s case count, and proof of delivery.


When those records show that the supplier shipped and delivered the full quantity, but the retailer’s records show otherwise, the deduction may be worth disputing. Comparing the retailer’s claim with the supplier’s shipment records can help determine whether the issue was an actual shortage or a receiving discrepancy.


## Physical Compliance Deductions


Shortage deductions focus on the difference between what shipped and what the retailer received. Physical compliance deductions result from the shipment itself failing to meet a retailer’s requirements.


Fashion retailers can be particularly specific about these requirements. Vendor compliance guides may spell out everything from approved hanger types and ticket placement to carton dimensions, weight limits, and labeling requirements.


### Hangers and Tickets


Von Maur’s[vendor compliance guide](https://www.vonmaur.com/VendorPolicy/48_2.pdf) requires hangers that meet current[Voluntary Interindustry Commerce Solutions (VICS) performance standards](https://www.gs1us.org/content/dam/gs1us/documents/industries-insights/by-industry/apparel-general-merchandise/guideline-toolkit/Guideline-GS1-US-Voluntary-Guidelines-for-Hanger-Specifications-for-Floor-Ready-Merchandise-R70.pdf) . Merchandise shipped without a compliant hanger can result in an offset expense.


Burlington’s[floor-ready requirements](https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hubfs/435785/BurlingtonCoat-FLOORREADY.pdf) are similarly specific. Its guidelines call for a 2-inch clear swift tag or a 5-inch clear loop lock on price tickets and require tickets to come through its designated ticket vendor. Loose or unattached tickets placed inside the carton, a practice sometimes called ticket seeding, don’t satisfy the requirement.


[Belk has additional requirements](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/belk-vendor-compliance-for-private-label-brands) for private-label merchandise. Since June 2021, private-label products shipped to Belk have required an RFID hangtag or sticker, with vendors directed to a specific RFID provider to meet the requirement.


These violations are largely preventable because retailers publish their requirements before suppliers ship. Suppliers can build those requirements into production and fulfillment processes before the first shipment leaves the facility.


They become disputable primarily when the retailer applies the deduction incorrectly, such as identifying the wrong shipment or product. If the supplier actually used a non-compliant hanger, there may be little basis for disputing the charge.


**Related Resource:** **[2D Barcode and RFID Readiness for Retail](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/unlock-your/2d-barcode-and-rfid-readiness-for-retail)


### Cartons and Labeling


Carton requirements follow a similar pattern. Von Maur’s guide establishes minimum and maximum carton dimensions and a 50-pound weight limit. Cartons that fall outside those requirements can incur an offset expense because oversized or overweight cartons may not move through the distribution center’s conveyor system as intended.


Barcode and GS1-128 labeling errors create a similar problem. A missing or unscannable label can interfere with automated receiving just as an improperly sized carton can interfere with material handling.


The prevention strategy for both is straightforward: Test cartons and labels against the retailer’s current requirements before the first shipment goes out. Suppliers should also double-check that they’re using the routing guide in effect on the shipment date, since retailer requirements can change.


## Use Deductions to Find Process Problems


The suppliers that recover more from deductions look for patterns, rather than dealing with each deduction as a separate issue.


When a deduction arrives, they compare it with their own shipment records before deciding whether to pay or dispute it. They also review deduction categories over time to identify recurring problems.


For example, a spike in shortage claims from a single distribution center could point to a receiving or reconciliation issue worth investigating. Tracking deductions by retailer, distribution center, deduction type, and root cause can help suppliers identify where process changes could prevent future losses.


There is evidence that compliance deductions can be incorrect at scale, rather than only in isolated disputes. In 2005, Saks disclosed that its audit committee had improperly collected roughly $20 million to $21.5 million in vendor markdown allowances between 1999 and 2003. The company[reimbursed affected vendors](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000812900/000119312505104302/dex991.htm) for those amounts, plus roughly $14 million in interest.


The audit committee also conducted a[supplemental inquiry](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000812900/000119312505174647/dex991.htm) into whether Saks had improperly charged vendors compliance chargebacks related to logistics, transportation, or billing policy failures.


Most deductions are legitimate and reflect a real operational issue, but can be issued incorrectly. Suppliers that maintain strong shipment and compliance documentation are in a better position to identify discrepancies and support a dispute when the retailer’s records don’t match their own.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the difference between a preventable and disputable deduction?


A preventable deduction is one a supplier can avoid through an operational or process change, such as using the correct hanger or keeping one purchase order per carton.


A disputable deduction is one the supplier can challenge after the fact because its documentation shows the deduction is incorrect. An ASN or signed BOL, for example, can help demonstrate that a shortage claim doesn’t match what actually shipped.


Many deductions fall into both categories. A supplier may be able to dispute the current deduction while also changing its process to prevent the same issue from happening again.


### Why do shortage claims make up so much of the deduction total?


A shortage claim occurs whenever a retailer’s receiving count is lower than the quantity the supplier invoiced. That difference can result from an actual short shipment, but it can also stem from commingled purchase orders, receiving errors, or discrepancies between the physical shipment and its paperwork.


Because there are so many potential causes, shortage claims make up a significant share of off-invoice deductions across the industry.


### What documents support retailer deduction disputes?


The right documentation depends on the type of deduction.


For most shortage disputes, the ASN, signed BOL with a driver-noted case count, and proof of delivery provide evidence of what was shipped and delivered.


For physical compliance deductions involving hangers, tickets, or labeling, relevant documentation may include a packing slip, carton contents record, vendor specification, or the retailer’s routing and compliance guide showing that the shipment met the applicable requirements.
